kp.k: Application companies can pursue task-specific frontier intelligence
kp.d: Pereyra argues that application companies can compensate for frontier labs' greater resources by using external training, infrastructure and model providers. He claims strong open-source models now make post-training competitive for specific legal tasks, unlike earlier periods when pre-training advances quickly absorbed its benefits. This is a founder's strategic assessment, not a quantified comparison of model performance.
qs: The frontier labs have more money, more talent, more compute infrastructure, and data. So how do you compete? By using the frontier ecosystem.
In the past, it wasn't worth doing post training because the models were improving so quickly from pre-training that any post training you did quickly got absorbed by the next pre-trained model.
Maybe not general frontier intelligence, but if you have a specific task like us, they are competitive.

kp.k: Benchmarks target associate, in-house negotiation and diligence tasks
kp.d: Pereyra reports releasing three datasets during the year of the talk: Legal Agent Bench, covering large-firm associate tasks across practice areas; a contracting dataset for in-house-style negotiation; and a diligence dataset whose largest data rooms contain 80 million tokens. He presents these as foundations for training and benchmarking complex legal work, not evidence that models can already perform all those tasks.
qs: So, this year we released three of these data sets that we built.
We started by building Legal Agent Bench, which is a taxonomy of tasks that associates would do at a large law firm.
This allows us to teach agents to do negotiation like you would in an in-house department.
The largest data rooms here are 80 million tokens, and it lets us do research on long context, very complex tasks.

kp.k: Client confidentiality constrains legal model training
kp.d: Pereyra says Harvey cannot train either generic or its own models on customers' sensitive, privileged legal data. Public final agreements do not supply the underlying transaction inputs needed for training. He describes domain-expert-guided synthetic generation as an approach that began working well that year, while explicitly acknowledging that synthetic data alone is insufficient.
qs: One challenge we always had at Harvey for training models is we can't train on our customers' data.
It's privileged, and so you can't put it in generic models. We can't even put it in our models.
you can maybe find some of the final work product publicly, so like a public purchase agreement, but you don't have any of the input data.
And once you've done that, synthetic data isn't good enough, but it's a way to get started.

kp.k: Lawyers construct synthetic matters around planted legal issues
kp.d: Pereyra describes Harvey lawyers using coding models to generate realistic training and product-evaluation datasets. For diligence, the process begins with a rubric and known issues, generates a mutually consistent data room around them, and uses external human augmentation to improve realism. A model's diligence memo can then be checked against the planted issues. He contrasts this with the difficulty of manually creating data rooms that can contain 10,000 contracts.
qs: He's trained our other lawyers to do that, and they can generate incredibly realistic data sets that we can use for training and also evaluating our product.
Because these data rooms can be 10,000 contracts. They all need to fit together.
And so he started from the rubric
Hey, did you catch all of these issues that we know that are in here because we planted them?

kp.k: Realistic legal matters still challenge frontier models
kp.d: Asked whether rubrics must deliberately separate frontier models, Pereyra instead prioritizes realistic representations of customer work. He asserts that realistic matters from top firms remain beyond frontier models' capabilities and credits lawyers' accumulated experience with models for improving dataset design. This is his qualitative assessment rather than a reported benchmark score.
qs: So, we think of it more as how do we make them realistic representations of the work our customers are doing?
if you just build a realistic client matter that these top firms are working on, like the frontier model still can't do this.
And so, he's been working with the models for 4 years.

kp.k: Large legal training environments make automated grading expensive
kp.d: Pereyra reports that the diligence dataset contains over 1,000 unit tests using LLM-as-judge grading. Running large models through reinforcement-learning rollouts makes this expensive, motivating work with LangChain to make the environments more efficient. These are training and evaluation mechanisms, not claims about human verification of client-facing legal work.
qs: For example, in our diligence data set, we have over 1,000 unit tests that are grading model outputs using LLM as a judge.
If you use the largest models and you want to do RL rollouts and things like this, it gets very expensive.
And so, there's a lot of work, and here's some we did with LangChain, of making these very efficient.

kp.k: Open benchmarks support scrutiny and external research collaboration
kp.d: Pereyra defends releasing some datasets as a way to discover defects, receive suggestions, encourage labs to benchmark models and let outside companies test techniques without consuming Harvey's internal research bandwidth. He acknowledges the strategic tension in helping other labs improve, but argues that explaining model differences to legal customers and enabling private customer systems are valuable.
qs: it's very hard to know your data set is good unless a lot of people train on it.
we get a ton of pull requests, we get suggestions.
every customer has different preferences, different models are good at different things.
the valuable data for us is going to be helping law firms train their own systems and how they work on private data.

kp.k: Research partnerships expand capacity and reduce infrastructure barriers
kp.d: Pereyra recommends beginning post-training with specialist external labs that provide expertise, recipes and infrastructure. Harvey uses multiple partners because projects exceed internal capacity and partners pursue different research approaches. He says available training and serving infrastructure also broadens the recruitable talent pool, while conceding Harvey is not competing for the highest-end frontier talent.
qs: we have more research projects than we have bandwidth to do internally or just with a single Neo lab.
And every Neo lab is taking a different bet. They have different ways they think about research.
we're not competing with kind of the frontier talent
you don't need to build the training and serving infrastructure, and so I think it opens up the pool of talent

kp.k: Production readiness requires more than strong benchmark performance
kp.d: Pereyra describes serving models across 60 countries, multiple products and customer preferences, with provider fallbacks to meet service commitments. Before deployment, Harvey combines automated benchmarks, human comparisons, product-specific tests and human product testing with cost, latency and regional availability. After deployment it uses A/B testing, engagement, uptime, token efficiency and customer feedback. He recommends establishing this infrastructure before post-training.
qs: we operate in 60 countries.
We need to have fallbacks across providers to hit our SLAs.
a model could be very good generically, but it could not be a good fit for a specific product surface.
And together these signals along with heuristics around cost, latency, region availability is how we decide whether we put a model into production.
We do AB testing if we're rolling out a large change, we look at engagement to track if this model's performing how we expect.

kp.k: Model substitution and routing precede proprietary post-training
kp.d: Pereyra recommends first finding product components where open-source models can directly replace larger models, citing citation generation as one opportunity for cost or performance benefits. Selective query routing is a second step where wholesale replacement is unsuitable. This builds operational experience serving open- and closed-source models together before introducing post-trained models; the talk supplies no quantified savings.
qs: we have parts of our product that generate citations that don't need the largest models
And so that's the first thing and doing this builds the muscle of serving open-source models alongside closed-source models.
there could be places where you can't naively swap an open-source model, but what you can do is on certain queries route to open-source models.

kp.k: Benchmark overfitting and production mismatch remain unresolved
kp.d: Pereyra cautions that models can score well on Harvey's benchmarks yet fail in a more general assistant when requests fall outside the training distribution. He identifies a gap between future-facing synthetic diligence tasks and actual product uses, such as email drafting, compounded by inability to inspect customer data. He also says models poorly manage the largest 80-million-token data rooms, leaving substantial performance gaps.
qs: you can have a model that does very well on our benchmarks, but they've overfit to some degree, and then you put it in a more generic assistant-like product, and it kind of falls apart for when you go out of distribution.
the distribution of that data still doesn't match our production distribution.
if a model does well on that, but then someone uses it to draft an email, maybe it doesn't work as well.
the largest data room is 80 million tokens of context. Like the models don't do a good job of managing this context

kp.k: Privacy-preserving customer customization is a longer-term goal
kp.d: Pereyra distinguishes current user-testing feedback that informs future datasets from training on customer data. His longer-term aim is continual learning tailored to each law firm or enterprise, with systems improving from successive client matters while protecting client information. He presents operationalizing this as an unresolved technical and operational challenge, not an established capability.
qs: In our case, it does not mean training on customer data, but we do get feedback signals from our user testing and other things that can inform how we build future data sets and improve these models.
the end game here is not for us to build the best legal model. It's for us to help every law firm or enterprise customer customize it to the type of work they're doing.
every time they work on a client matter, their AI system gets better, but you're also protecting the client data.

kp.k: Harvey targets organizational rather than individual legal productivity
kp.d: Pereyra describes a strategic shift from individual drafting assistance toward coordinating long-running matters, teams, outside parties and agents. His illustrative scenarios include a firm with 10,000 clients, a six-month matter involving 20–30 people, and an enterprise coordinating a thousand law firms and a thousand internal people; these are examples, not measured customer populations. He sees domain-specific project management, resource allocation, billing and pitching as differentiation from horizontal products, with successful and profitable client projects as the organizational objective.
qs: And increasingly, the product we're building is about organizational productivity.
I need to make sure that all those client projects go very well, and then I can also do them in a way that's profitable.
a lot of it is starting to look like project management that is orchestrating these humans and these agents.
you need to start thinking about resource allocation, what am I billing, what am I pitching?
how do you just go hyper vertical into your domain in a way that the horizontal products won't.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Gabriel Pereyra describes a shift toward task-specialised legal AI, customer-specific learning and organisation-wide coordination of legal work, while acknowledging substantial remaining capability gaps.
pts.d: Pereyra makes several connected claims. First, application-layer companies such as Harvey can now use external training and serving infrastructure and strong open-source models to compete with frontier laboratories on specific tasks, rather than on general intelligence. Second, lawyer-guided synthetic data generation makes it possible to train and benchmark systems on complex legal work without training on Harvey customers' confidential data. He describes datasets covering large-firm associate work, in-house contract negotiation and large-scale diligence. Third, selectively substituting or routing requests to open-source models can provide cost or performance benefits; citation generation is his example of a component that does not require the largest models. Fourth, open benchmarks help customers understand differences among models, enable external researchers to test improvements and support collaboration with model laboratories. He rejects the premise that one best model will satisfy all legal customers. Fifth, Harvey's longer-term aim is to help each law firm or enterprise customise its AI to its own work, potentially improving with each client matter while protecting client data; he presents this continual-learning capability as an unresolved goal, not an achieved feature. Sixth, he says Harvey is moving beyond individual lawyer productivity toward organisational productivity: coordinating humans and agents across matters, external parties, staffing, billing and pitching. He positions deep legal-domain specialisation as a way to compete with horizontal AI products. Separately, he predicts that every company will need to become an AI company and develop some version of this approach. He does not predict lawyer headcount reductions, changes to partnership structures or improvements in access to justice.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The supporting basis is primarily Pereyra's account of Harvey's internal development and production experience, with concrete dataset descriptions but no reported comparative performance or productivity results.
pts.d: Pereyra reports three datasets released that year: Legal Agent Bench, a contracting dataset and a diligence dataset. He gives scale indicators of up to 80 million tokens in a diligence data room and more than 1,000 unit tests grading outputs through LLM judges. These describe the training and benchmarking setup, not measured legal accuracy. In the Q&A, he explains a rubric-first method: lawyers specify and plant issues, generate a coherent fictional data room, refine document realism with external assistance, and test whether a generated diligence memo identifies the planted issues. He reports that these demonstrations have prompted law-firm interest in training on their own data, without naming customers or documenting resulting deployments. He also cites collaboration with infrastructure and research partners, an established production product, operations in 60 countries and a multi-stage model-selection process. That process includes automated benchmarks, human side-by-side comparisons, product-specific tests, deployment A/B tests, engagement, uptime, token efficiency and customer feedback. These are model and product evaluation signals, not evidence of human verification of every legal output before reliance. His claims about task-level frontier competitiveness, cheaper or better model substitution and broader recruitment possibilities are experiential assertions without benchmark scores, cost comparisons or hiring statistics. The proposed organisational-productivity shift and continual learning are supported by descriptions of customer workflow problems and strategic intent, not quantified evidence of improved matter outcomes or profitability. The transcript contains unreliable proper nouns, so model and partner names should not be treated as independently verified.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Pereyra distinguishes recent technical opportunities from future ambitions and conditions deployment on confidentiality, realistic data, product-level testing and infrastructure readiness.
pts.d: In the talk dated 11 August 2026 by the supplied document, Pereyra refers to four years of Harvey development and describes expert-guided synthetic generation and the three dataset releases as developments of 'this year'. He contrasts the present opportunity for task-specific post-training with an earlier period when rapid base-model improvements overtook the gains from custom training. He says shared infrastructure now reduces the need to recruit rare researchers capable of building the entire training and serving stack. These opportunities are qualified: Harvey cannot train on customer data, synthetic data alone is insufficient, and synthetic training distributions do not match actual production use. His diligence environments are partly future-facing rather than a complete reflection of current product use. A model can perform well on a benchmark yet fail in a general assistant setting or on a task such as drafting an email; frontier models still cannot complete realistic complex top-firm matters, and handling very large contexts remains a major performance gap. Production adoption requires task-specific and human testing as well as attention to cost, latency, regional availability, reliability and feedback. Customer feedback can inform future dataset construction but does not mean customer-data training. Continual learning on private matters and the organisation-wide orchestration vision have no specified completion date. His reference to future firm-specific training should therefore be distinguished from his account of Harvey's current prohibition on training on customer data.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are large law firms, their lawyers and clients, enterprise legal departments, and the legal-AI development ecosystem.
pts.d: For large law firms and associates, Pereyra describes systems trained around drafting, legal research and diligence, with an intended progression from assistance on individual tasks to coordination of whole matters and firm-wide resources. His examples of 20–30 people on a six-month matter and thousands of concurrent projects illustrate coordination demands rather than measured AI effects. For enterprise legal departments, he describes negotiation training and the longer-term challenge of coordinating internal personnel, external law firms and work-management systems. For clients, confidentiality and privilege constrain training; the proposed benefit is better-run matters that remain profitable for the provider, not a demonstrated reduction in client fees. Lawyers employed by Harvey take on an expert role in designing rubrics, guiding synthetic-data generation and building realistic evaluation environments. AI researchers and application companies are affected by lower infrastructure barriers and an expanded potential hiring pool; external laboratories and developers can use open datasets to test techniques and improve models. Harvey's strategic opportunity, in Pereyra's account, is to provide customer-specific systems and deeply specialised organisational infrastructure rather than merely a generic chat interface. The discussion concerns predominantly large-firm and enterprise practice, not consumer legal aid or unmet civil legal need.
